steps.explain: Why the other answers are wrong: one shifts every digit one place (so the number is ten times too big or small), one has the digits swapped around the decimal point, and one reverses the digits.

keyPoints.note: Each place is ten times the place to its right.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals
meta.note: Chart columns are written as H = hundreds, T = tens, O = ones, t = tenths, h = hundredths, th = thousandths.

questions.stem: Which expanded form is equal to \(87.46\)?
questions.hint: Write each digit's place value: tens, ones, tenths, hundredths, ...

steps.explain: Expanded form writes each digit with its place value, then adds them.

questions.stem: Write the decimal number \(29.487\) on a place-value chart.
questions.hint: Digits to the left of the point: ones, tens, hundreds. Digits to the right: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

steps.explain: A place-value chart has a column for every place. To the LEFT of the decimal point: Hundreds, Tens, Ones. To the RIGHT of the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

keyPoints.note: Each place is ten times the place to its right.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

steps.explain: Change the fraction part to a decimal. If the denominator is 10, 100 or 1000 the digits come straight from the numerator. Otherwise first make an equivalent fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 (multiply top and bottom by the same number).
2 goes into 10 exactly 5 times, so use denominator 10: multiply the top and bottom by 5.
The whole number 1 stays as the whole-number part.
The denominator 10 has 1 zero, so the decimal has 1 decimal place. Write the numerator 5 with 1 digit after the point (put zeros in front if needed).

steps.explain: Count the decimal places: 05 has 2 digits after the point, so the denominator is 1 followed by 2 zeros: 100.
The numerator is the digits after the point: \(05 = 5\).
Simplify: the highest common factor of 5 and 100 is 5. Divide the top and bottom by 5.
Check by changing the fraction back to a decimal: divide the numerator by the denominator.
Why the other answers are wrong: they use the wrong denominator (too many or too few zeros), swap the numerator and denominator, or change the whole number.

keyPoints.note: A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

questions.stem: Order the following numbers from greatest to least: \\(5.69, 5.7, 5.71\\).
questions.hint: Compare the digits in the tenths and hundredths places. You can write 5.7 as 5.70 to make comparison easier.

steps.explain: To compare these numbers easily, write each number with the same number of decimal places by adding trailing zeros where needed.
Now compare the decimal parts: 71 hundredths is larger than 70 hundredths, which is larger than 69 hundredths.
Ordering from greatest to least, we get 5.71 first, then 5.7 (or 5.70), and finally 5.69.

questions.stem: Order the following numbers from greatest to least: \\(3.47, 3.45, 3.54\\).
questions.hint: Compare the tenths digit first. 3.54 has 5 in the tenths place, while the others have 4.

steps.explain: We compare the tenths digit of each number. 3.54 has a tenths digit of 5, while 3.47 and 3.45 have a tenths digit of 4. Therefore, 3.54 is the largest.
Next, compare the remaining numbers 3.47 and 3.45 by looking at their hundredths digits. 7 hundredths is greater than 5 hundredths.
Putting them together from greatest to least gives us 3.54, then 3.47, and lastly 3.45.

questions.stem: Order the following numbers from least to greatest: \\(4.7, 4.07, 4.72, 4.27, 4.702\\).
questions.hint: Write all numbers with three decimal places (e.g. write 4.7 as 4.700) to make it easy to compare them.

steps.explain: Write each decimal out to 3 decimal places so they have the same length.
Compare the decimal parts: 070 (smallest) < 270 < 700 < 702 < 720 (largest).
Arrange the original numbers in order from least to greatest.

questions.stem: Order the following numbers from greatest to least: \\(1.34, 1.04, 1.4, 1.304, 1.403\\).
questions.hint: Convert all decimals to three decimal places by appending zeros (e.g. write 1.4 as 1.400) to compare values easily.

steps.explain: Pad each decimal number with trailing zeros so that they all have three decimal digits.
Compare the decimal parts: 403 (largest) > 400 > 340 > 304 > 040 (smallest).
Order the original numbers from greatest to least according to their compared decimal values.

questions.stem: Put these decimals in order, smallest first: \(7.426,\ 7.845,\ 7.417\)
questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, add zeros so all numbers have the same number of places, compare from the left.

steps.explain: To compare decimals, line up the DECIMAL POINTS and write zeros on the end so every number has the same number of decimal places (this does not change the value).
After the zeros are added, the numbers are: 7.426, 7.845, 7.417. Now they can be compared like whole numbers.
Compare place by place from the LEFT: look at the biggest place first. The number with the bigger digit in the first place where they differ is bigger.
Order the padded numbers: 7.417 < 7.426 < 7.845.
Write the numbers as they were originally given (without the extra zeros), in this order.

Why the other answers are wrong: one is in the opposite order, one orders by the number of decimal places (a longer decimal is not always bigger), one orders by ignoring the decimal point, and one swaps two neighbours.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and compare place by place from the left.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

steps.explain: Line up the decimal numbers vertically so that identical place values are aligned.
Add the digits in the hundredths column: 3 + 5 = 8.
Add the digits in the tenths column: 7 + 1 = 8.
Add the digits in the units column: 6 + 2 = 8. Place the decimal point in the same relative position.

questions.hint: Make sure to carry over 1 to the units place when adding the tenths (9 + 3 = 12).

Add the hundredths column: 2 + 5 = 7.
Add the tenths column: 9 + 3 = 12. Write down 2 in the tenths place and carry over 1 to the units column.
Add the units column, including the carry: 4 + 1 + 1 = 6.

questions.hint: This addition involves carrying digits in both the hundredths and tenths columns.

steps.explain: Set up the vertical addition with aligned decimal places.
Add the hundredths column: 4 + 9 = 13. Write 3 in the hundredths place and carry 1 to the tenths column.

Add the units column: 5 + 8 + 1 (carry) = 14.

questions.hint: Align the decimal points vertically, and add columns from right to left.

steps.explain: Set up vertical addition.
Add the hundredths column: 2 + 5 = 7. Then add the tenths column: 7 + 4 = 11 (write 1, carry 1).
Add the units column, including the carry: 6 + 2 + 1 = 9. Finally, add the tens column: 8 + 1 = 9.

questions.hint: Pay close attention to carrying numbers over to the next column when adding.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and add column by column; carry when needed.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

steps.explain: Line up the numbers so the DECIMAL POINTS are in a straight line (one under the other), so that tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths and so on.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and add column by column; carry when needed.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, add zeros so every number has the same number of places, then add column by column from the right.

steps.explain: Line up the numbers so the DECIMAL POINTS are in a straight line (one under the other), so that tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths and so on.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and add column by column; carry when needed.
A decimal with n places is a fraction with denominator 10, 100 or 1000 and so on.

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, add zeros so every number has the same number of places, then add column by column from the right.

steps.explain: Line up the numbers so the DECIMAL POINTS are in a straight line (one under the other), so that tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths and so on.

questions.hint: Align the decimal points vertically, and subtract column by column starting from the right.

steps.explain: Write the problem vertically, aligning the decimal points.
Subtract the tenths column: 9 - 5 = 4.
Subtract the units column: 3 - 2 = 1. Insert the decimal point in the correct vertical position.

questions.hint: Since 4 is less than 6, you need to borrow 1 unit from the units place (8) to make it 14 tenths.

steps.explain: Arrange the subtraction vertically with aligned decimal points.
Since we cannot subtract 6 from 4 in the tenths column, borrow 1 unit from the units digit 8 (leaving 7). This turns the 4 tenths into 14 tenths.
Subtract the units column (now 7 - 3): 7 - 3 = 4.

questions.hint: Borrow 1 unit from the units column to subtract the tenths column (12 tenths minus 7 tenths).

steps.explain: Align the numbers vertically.
Borrow 1 from the units place (reducing 9 to 8) to convert the 2 tenths into 12 tenths. Then subtract: 12 - 7 = 5.
Subtract the units digits (now 8 - 4): 8 - 4 = 4.

questions.hint: Line up decimal places. Subtract each column from right to left.

steps.explain: Write the subtraction vertically.
Subtract hundredths: 9 - 3 = 6. Subtract tenths: 7 - 4 = 3.
Subtract units: 6 - 1 = 5. Subtract tens: 1 - 0 = 1.

questions.hint: Borrow 1 from the tenths digit (6) to subtract 8 from 5 in the hundredths column.

steps.explain: Set up subtraction vertically.
Borrow 1 from tenths place (reducing 6 to 5) to make 15 hundredths. Subtract: 15 - 8 = 7. Subtract tenths: 5 - 1 = 4.
Subtract whole numbers: 34 - 7 = 27.

questions.hint: Set up columns and subtract. You will need to borrow to subtract the tenths column (2 - 5).

steps.explain: Set up subtraction vertically.
Subtract hundredths: 9 - 8 = 1. To subtract tenths, borrow 1 from units (4 becomes 3) to make 12 tenths. Subtract: 12 - 5 = 7.
Subtract units (3 - 7 requires borrowing from tens, so 13 - 7 = 6). Subtract tens: 5 - 1 = 4.

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points and perform vertical subtraction, borrowing where necessary.

steps.explain: Align the numbers vertically.
Subtract cents column: 7 - 8 requires borrowing (17 - 8 = 9). 3 - 1 = 2.
Subtract dollars column: 3 - 9 requires borrowing (13 - 9 = 4). 7 - 6 = 1. 1 - 0 = 1.

questions.hint: Set up subtraction vertically, and borrow from the units digit (8) to subtract the tenths digit.

steps.explain: Align decimal points vertically.
Subtract hundredths column: 5 - 3 = 2.
Borrow 1 unit from units place (8 becomes 7) to make 13 tenths. Subtract: 13 - 9 = 4.
Subtract units (7 - 4 = 3) and tens (6 - 1 = 5).

questions.hint: Borrow 1 from the tenths digit (2) to subtract the hundredths column.

steps.explain: Write vertical columns.
Borrow from tenths (2 becomes 1) to make 11 hundredths. Subtract: 11 - 8 = 3. Subtract tenths: 1 - 1 = 0.
Subtract units: 7 - 3 = 4. Subtract tens (borrowing from hundreds): 15 - 6 = 9. Hundreds: 2.

questions.hint: Set up subtraction vertically. You will need to borrow in both the hundredths and units columns.

steps.explain: Align columns vertically.
Borrow from tenths (7 becomes 6) to make 12 hundredths. Subtract: 12 - 5 = 7. Subtract tenths: 6 - 1 = 5.
Borrow from tens (9 becomes 8) to make 16 units. Subtract: 16 - 8 = 8. Subtract tens: 8 - 3 = 5. Subtract hundreds: 4 - 1 = 3.

questions.hint: Set up subtraction vertically. Write $100 as $100.00 and borrow across zeros.

steps.explain: Align the digits vertically, writing $100 with cents places.
Borrow across the zeros from the hundreds place. The units digit becomes 9, and the last digit becomes 10.
Subtract columns from right to left: 10 - 2 = 8, 9 - 7 = 2, 9 - 6 = 3, 9 - 1 = 8.

questions.hint: Write vertically and borrow across columns starting from the right.

steps.explain: Line up by decimal points.
Subtract hundredths: 5 - 7 requires borrowing (15 - 7 = 8). Subtract tenths: (2 - 4 requires borrowing, so 12 - 4 = 8).
Subtract units (1 - 6 requires borrowing, so 11 - 6 = 5). Subtract tens: 6 - 1 = 5.

questions.hint: Set up vertical subtraction. Make sure you align the units digit 8 of $48 under the 0 of $130.

steps.explain: Set up vertical subtraction.
Subtract hundredths: borrow from tenths (7 becomes 17, 4 becomes 3). 17 - 9 = 8. Subtract tenths: 3 - 2 = 1.
Subtract whole dollars: 130 - 48 = 82.

questions.hint: Subtract the second number first, then subtract the third number from the result.

steps.explain: Perform the first subtraction: $49.53 - $6.41.
Perform the second subtraction: subtract $12.85 from $43.12.
Borrow where needed. 12 - 5 = 7 (hundredths). 10 - 8 = 2 (tenths). 42 - 12 = 30 (dollars).

questions.hint: Subtract 5.8 from 13.72. Pad 5.8 as 5.80 to keep place values aligned.

steps.explain: Write the decrease as a subtraction expression.
Set up vertical subtraction, adding a zero placeholder to 5.8.
Subtract the columns: 2 - 0 = 2. 7 - 8 requires borrowing (17 - 8 = 9). 12 - 5 = 7.

questions.hint: Subtract 3.94 from 18.01 using vertical columns.

steps.explain: Express the difference as a subtraction sentence.
Set up vertical subtraction.
Borrow across columns to complete the subtraction: 11 - 4 = 7. 9 - 9 = 0. 17 - 3 = 14.

questions.stem: A logistics courier has a daily budget of \\(\$50.00\\) for dispatch expenses. They spend \\(\$18.35\\) on fuel refills, \\(\$8.49\\) on road tolls, and \\(\$4.38\\) on package sealing tape. How much of the daily budget remains?
questions.hint: Find the total amount spent by adding the three individual expenses together, then subtract this total from the initial budget of \\(\$50.00\\).

steps.explain: First, identify the initial budget and list all the individual expenses. The initial budget is \\(\$50.00\\), and the expenses are \\(\$18.35\\), \\(\$8.49\\), and \\(\$4.38\\).
Add the three expenses together to find the total amount spent. Align the decimal points vertically to ensure accurate addition of cents and dollars.
Subtract the total expenses of \\(\$31.22\\) from the initial budget of \\(\$50.00\\) to determine the remaining amount. Again, align the decimal points and perform the subtraction.
Verify that the final calculated difference represents the remaining budget. The logistics courier has \\(\$18.78\\) left in their daily budget.

questions.stem: An environmental volunteer team allocates a budget of \\(\$20.00\\) for planting supplies. A volunteer spends \\(\$1.68\\) on biodegradable seed bags, \\(\$3.45\\) on organic fertilizer tablets, and \\(70\\) cents on compost labels. How much budget remains?
questions.hint: Ensure all values are in the same currency unit. Note that \\(70\\) cents is equivalent to \\(\$0.70\\). Sum the expenses and subtract from \\(\$20.00\\).

steps.explain: Identify the starting budget and convert the 70 cents expense into dollars so that all quantities are in the same unit. This is necessary before performing any addition.
Add all three individual expenses together. Make sure to align the decimal points: \\(\$1.68\\) for seed bags, \\(\$3.45\\) for fertilizer, and \\(\$0.70\\) for labels.
Subtract the total spent of \\(\$5.83\\) from the initial budget of \\(\$20.00\\). Align the decimal points and perform the subtraction.
Confirm the remaining budget in dollars. The environmental volunteer team has \\(\$14.17\\) remaining.

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths. Write zeros on the end of the shorter number so both numbers have the same number of decimal places (the value does not change).

steps.explain: Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column; trade when needed.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 8: Decimals

questions.hint: Line up the decimal points, write zeros so both numbers have the same number of places, then subtract column by column (trade when you need to).

steps.explain: Subtracting means taking away. Put the bigger number on top and line up the DECIMAL POINTS so tenths are under tenths, hundredths under hundredths.

questions.hint: When multiplying a decimal by 10, shift the decimal point one position to the right.

steps.explain: Identify the multiplier. Since we are multiplying by 10 (which has one zero), we shift the decimal point one place to the right.
Perform the shift on the decimal number 7.31.

questions.hint: When multiplying by 1000 (three zeros), shift the decimal point three positions to the right, adding placeholder zeros if needed.

steps.explain: Count the number of zeros in 1000. There are 3 zeros, meaning we must move the decimal point three places to the right.
Move the decimal point on 6.32. After moving two places, it becomes 632. We must add one trailing zero placeholder to complete the three-place shift.

questions.hint: Multiplying by 100 shifts the decimal point two places to the right.

steps.explain: Identify the number of zeros in 100. There are two zeros, so move the decimal point two places to the right.
Perform the decimal shift on the number 4.089.

questions.hint: Shift the decimal point one place to the right. Remember to include the trailing zero for cents format.

steps.explain: Since we are multiplying by 10, shift the decimal point one position to the right.
Perform the shift: 7.42 becomes 74.2.
Format the value as money by adding a trailing zero in the hundredths place to show cents.

questions.hint: Multiplying by 10, 100, 1000 moves the decimal point 1, 2, 3 places right; dividing moves it left. Add zeros if you run out of digits.

steps.explain: To multiply by 10 we move the decimal point 1 place to the RIGHT (every digit becomes ten times bigger each place).

questions.hint: Shift the decimal point two positions to the left because you are dividing by 100.

steps.explain: Since 100 contains two zeros, we must shift the decimal point of the dividend two places to the left.
Perform the decimal shift on the number 816.9.

questions.hint: Divide by 1000 by shifting the decimal point three positions to the left, adding a leading placeholder zero.

steps.explain: Division by 1000 (three zeros) requires shifting the decimal point three places to the left.
Move the decimal point on 27.35. Since there are only two digits to the left of the decimal, add one leading zero as a placeholder.

questions.hint: Shift the decimal point one place to the left because you are dividing by 10.

steps.explain: To divide by 10, shift the decimal point one place to the left.

questions.stem: A specialized 3D printing service charges \\(\$7.42\\) per hour of machine operation. How much in dollars will a client be charged for a print job that requires exactly \\(35\\) hours of continuous operation?
questions.hint: Multiply the hourly charge rate of \\(\$7.42\\) by the total duration of \\(35\\) hours.

steps.explain: Identify the hourly charge and the total hours to calculate the overall cost. The hourly rate is \\(\$7.42\\), and the total duration is \\(35\\) hours.
Set up the multiplication of the decimal number \\(7.42\\) and the whole number \\(35\\).
Multiply the digits: \\(742 \\times 35 = 25970\\). Since the factor 7.42 has two decimal places, place the decimal point two digits from the right of 25970.
Conclude with the final cost in dollars. The client will be charged \\(\$259.70\\) for the printing service.

steps.explain: Multiply as if there were NO decimal point: write the decimal point away and multiply the whole numbers. Then put the decimal point back by counting decimal places.
Ignore the decimal point: 0.098 becomes 98 (it had 3 decimal places).
Multiply 98 by the ones digit 9 of 9: \(8\times 9=72\); \(9\times 9+7=88\). The row is 882.
Count decimal places: only 0.098 has decimals (3 places), and 9 has none, so the answer has 3 decimal places. Count 3 digits in from the RIGHT of 882 and put the decimal point there.

steps.explain: Divide the first two digits: 13 divided by 5 is 2, remainder 3.

Carry 1 to the tenths column to make 15 tenths. Divide: 15 divided by 5 is 3.

Carry the remainder 6 to the tenths place to make 60. 60 divided by 9 is 6, remainder 6.

questions.hint: Divide 33 by 7 to find the whole dollars and carry the remainder.

steps.explain: Divide whole dollars: 33 divided by 7 is 4, remainder 5.

Carry 1 to make 14 hundredths. Divide: 14 divided by 7 is 2.

questions.hint: Divide by 12. Check how many times 12 goes into 104 first.

steps.explain: Divide whole dollars: 104 divided by 12 is 8, remainder 8 (since 12 x 8 = 96).
Carry 8 to make 87 tenths. 87 divided by 12 is 7, remainder 3 (since 12 x 7 = 84).

questions.stem: A community greenhouse receives a utility bill of \\(\$334\\) for a heating pump that ran continuously for \\(40\\) hours. What is the average operating cost of the heating pump per hour?
questions.hint: Divide the total utility bill of \\(\$334\\) by the total operating time of \\(40\\) hours.

steps.explain: Identify the total cost and hours to find the hourly rate. The total cost is \\(\$334\\), and the duration is \\(40\\) hours.
Set up the division of the total cost by the number of hours. This can be simplified by dividing by 10 first, then by 4.
Divide the numerator and denominator by 10 to simplify the fraction. This makes the divisor a single digit.
Perform long division of \\(33.4\\) by \\(4\\) to get the final decimal quotient.
Express the result in currency terms. The average operating cost of the heating pump is \\(\$8.35\\) per hour.

steps.explain: Set out the division like a whole-number division. Write the decimal point of the answer directly ABOVE the decimal point of the number being divided, and keep the digits in line.

steps.explain: Divide the ones digit: how many lots of 6 are in 7? 1 lots, because \(1 \times 6 = 6\) (and \(2 \times 6 = 12\) is too big). Write 1 above, subtract: \(7 - 6 = 1\). Next comes the decimal point: write it in the answer straight above the point.

keyPoints.note: Divide as whole numbers; keep the decimal point aligned.

keyPoints.note: Divide as whole numbers; keep the decimal point aligned.

questions.stem: A rope \(132.5\) m long is cut into 5 equal pieces. How long is each piece?
questions.hint: Put the decimal point of the answer straight above the point in the number, and write zeros on the end if the division does not finish.

steps.explain: Set out the division like a whole-number division. Write the decimal point of the answer directly ABOVE the decimal point of the number being divided, and keep the digits in line.

questions.stem: A ribbon \(2.8\) m long is used for 4 equal sides. How long is each side?
questions.hint: Put the decimal point of the answer straight above the point in the number, and write zeros on the end if the division does not finish.

steps.explain: Set out the division like a whole-number division. Write the decimal point of the answer directly ABOVE the decimal point of the number being divided, and keep the digits in line.

questions.hint: Multiply 7 by 4. Since both decimal numbers have one decimal digit, the result must have two decimal digits.

steps.explain: First, multiply the numbers ignoring decimal points.
Count total decimal places in both factors. 0.7 has 1 and 0.4 has 1, which sum to 2 decimal places.
Place the decimal point in the product so that there are 2 places after it.

questions.hint: Multiply 5 by 3. Since both numbers have one decimal place, their product must have two decimal places.

steps.explain: Multiply the numbers ignoring decimal points.
Calculate the total decimal places. Each factor has one decimal place, which sums to two decimal places.
Insert the decimal point to show two decimal places.

questions.hint: Squaring a number means multiplying it by itself. Calculate 0.3 x 0.3.

steps.explain: Write the squared term as a product.
Multiply the numbers: 3 multiplied by 3 is 9. Count decimal places: 1 + 1 = 2.
Write the result with two decimal places using a placeholder zero.

questions.stem: Premium carbon fiber tape costs \\(\$4.70\\) per metre. How much will it cost an aerospace engineering team to purchase \\(8.5\\) metres of this tape?
questions.hint: Multiply the cost per metre by the total length required: \\(4.70 \\times 8.5\\).

steps.explain: First, identify the rate and the quantity to find the total cost. The rate is \\(\$4.70\\) per metre, and the total length is \\(8.5\\) metres.
Set up the multiplication of the decimal values. We can ignore the decimal points initially and multiply the integers, then place the decimal point.
Perform the multiplication \\(47 \\times 85 = 3995\\). Since there are two decimal places in total between the factors (one in 4.7 and one in 8.5), place the decimal point two digits from the right.
Write the final cost with the currency symbol. The total cost to buy 8.5 metres of carbon fiber tape is \\(\$39.95\\).

questions.stem: A chemical laboratory purchases high-grade liquid nitrogen at a rate of \\(\$8.40\\) per litre. What is the total cost in dollars to purchase exactly \\(1.3\\) litres of liquid nitrogen?
questions.hint: Multiply the price per litre by the number of litres: \\(8.40 \\times 1.3\\).

steps.explain: Identify the unit price and quantity required. The price is \\(\$8.40\\) per litre, and the quantity is \\(1.3\\) litres.
Set up the multiplication of the decimal values. You can drop the trailing zero in 8.40 to simplify the calculation.
Multiply the numbers as integers: \\(84 \\times 13 = 1092\\). Since the factors have two decimal places combined, place the decimal point two spaces from the right.
Confirm the final cost in dollars. The total cost of the liquid nitrogen is \\(\$10.92\\).

questions.stem: A solar energy storage system feeds electricity back into the grid, returning \\(32\\) cents of credit for every dollar value of energy produced. How much credit in dollars will a household receive if their total produced energy value is \\(\$350.00\\)?
questions.hint: Express the 32 cents tax/credit rate as a decimal value of \\(0.32\\) per dollar, then multiply by the total value of \\(\$350.00\\).

steps.explain: Identify the credit rate and the total energy value. The rate is \\(32\\) cents per dollar (which is \\(\$0.32\\) per dollar), and the total value is \\(\$350\\).
Set up the multiplication of the total energy value and the decimal rate. This determines the total credits earned.
Multiply the numbers as integers first: \\(350 \\times 32 = 11200\\). Since the rate has two decimal places, move the decimal point two places to the left.
Confirm the final credit amount. The household will receive a total credit of \\(\$112.00\\).

steps.explain: 'Of' means MULTIPLY. A decimal of an amount is the decimal times the amount.
Write 0.75 as a fraction: it has 2 decimal places, so the denominator is 100.
Multiply the amount by the numerator 75, then divide by 100.
Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point 2 places to the left.
Check: a decimal less than 1 gives an answer smaller than the amount, a decimal bigger than 1 gives an answer bigger.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

Multiply the amount by the numerator 25, then divide by 100.
Dividing by 100 moves the decimal point 2 places to the left.
Check: a decimal less than 1 gives an answer smaller than the amount, a decimal bigger than 1 gives an answer bigger.
Why the other answers are wrong: they come from putting the decimal point in the wrong place, not lining up the decimal points, or a slip in a column.

keyPoints.note: 'Of' means multiply: change the decimal to a fraction or use the algorithm.

questions.stem: Round off \\(\$3.476\\) to the nearest cent.
questions.hint: Cents are represented by the hundredths place (second decimal place). Look at the third digit (6) to decide whether to round up or down.

steps.explain: Identify the target rounding place value. Cents correspond to the hundredths place, which is the digit 7 in $3.476.
Inspect the digit in the thousandths place (the digit immediately to the right of the hundredths place), which is 6.
Round the hundredths digit up by 1 and truncate the following digits.

steps.explain: The rounding digit is 3. Look at the digit just to its RIGHT: it is 5.
If that digit is 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9 round UP (add 1 to the rounding digit); if it is 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 leave the rounding digit as it is. Here 5 is 5 or more, so round UP.
All the digits to the right of the rounding place are dropped (replaced by zeros when they are in front of the point).
So 235 rounded to the nearest ten is 240.
Why the other answers are wrong: they round the wrong way, round at the wrong place, or move the decimal point.

questions.stem: An industrial warehouse robot traverses a distance of \\(16.47\\) metres in \\(9\\) seconds. At this constant speed, how many metres will the robot travel in exactly one minute?
questions.hint: First find the speed of the robot per second by dividing \\(16.47\\) by \\(9\\). Then, multiply this speed by \\(60\\) seconds (one minute).

steps.explain: Identify the given values and plan the steps. The robot travels \\(16.47\\) metres in \\(9\\) seconds, and we need to find the distance traveled in \\(60\\) seconds.
Calculate the robot's speed per second by dividing the distance by the time. This gives the rate of travel in metres per second.
Multiply the speed by 60 to find the total distance covered in one minute (60 seconds). Multi-digit multiplication is used.
State the final conclusion with appropriate units. The warehouse robot will travel a total distance of 109.8 metres in one minute.
